brief: Secret Santa: n people each wish to give to a_i. Assign each giver a distinct receiver, never themselves, maximizing the number of givers who give to their wish.
key_idea: The answer is the number of distinct wish values; one giver per value gets its wish, the rest are paired and self-loops are repaired by a swap.
solution: Scan i=1..n; the first giver wishing value v gets b_i = v. Let k be the number of distinct values.
Unassigned givers G and unused receivers R have equal size m; set b[G[j]] = R[j].
For a giver i with b_i = i and m >= 2, swap b_i with the entry of another unassigned giver; this never creates a new self-loop.
If m = 1, let j be the giver holding value a_i; set b_i = a_i and b_j = i.
Print k and the assignment.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1 (n=3, a = 2 1 2): person 1 gets 2, person 2 gets 1, so k = 2.
G = {3}, R = {3}; b_3 = 3 is a self-loop and m = 1, so take j = 1 (holds value a_3 = 2).
Set b_3 = 2 and b_1 = 3; result b = 3 1 2 with k = 2, matching the sample.

brief: Tree Infection: a rooted tree on n vertices. Each second every vertex with an infected child may infect one more child, then you may infect one healthy vertex. Find the minimum number of seconds to infect all vertices.
key_idea: Groups are the child set of each vertex plus the root alone; infection spreads within a group, so binary search the time T with a feasibility check on sorted group sizes.
solution: Build groups: each vertex's child set (if non-empty) plus the singleton {1}. Let k be the number of groups, sorted sizes s_1 >= ... >= s_k.
Each group needs its own first injection, so T >= k.
Group i (1-indexed) is injected at time i and then gains one per second; with e_i extra injections it is complete iff 1 + (T - i) + e_i >= s_i.
The spare injections are T - k, so T is feasible iff sum over i of max(0, s_i - (T - i + 1)) <= T - k. This is monotone in T.
Binary search the smallest feasible T in [k, 2n+5].
complexity: O(n log n) time per test (sort plus binary search with O(k) checks), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2 (n=5, parents 5 5 1 4): child sets {2,3}, {4}, {5}, plus {1}; sorted sizes 2,1,1,1, so k = 4.
T = 4: i=1 term 2 - (4 - 1 + 1) < 0, so the need is 0 <= T - k = 0; feasible.
Answer 4, matching the sample.

brief: Basic Diplomacy: m days, each with a set of available friends. Pick one friend per day so that no friend is picked more than ceil(m/2) times, or print NO.
key_idea: Bipartite assignment with capacities: days to friends, each friend capacity ceil(m/2); a max flow that saturates every day gives a valid schedule.
solution: Build source -> day (cap 1), day -> each available friend (cap 1), friend -> sink (cap L = ceil(m/2)).
Run Dinic. If the max flow is less than m, print NO.
Otherwise each day's saturated edge gives its friend; print YES and the list.
The sink capacity guarantees no friend exceeds L picks.
complexity: O(E sqrt(V)) time with Dinic on this unit-capacity network (E = sum k_i + n + m), O(E) space
dry_run: Sample 2 (n=2, m=2, days {1} and {1}): L = 1, so friend 1 can take only one day.
Max flow = 1 < 2, so the output is NO, matching the sample.

brief: Beautiful Palindromes: given an array with values in [1,n], append exactly k values in [1,n] so that the total number of palindromic subarrays is minimal; output the appended values.
key_idea: Each appended value adds at least one palindrome (its own single character); values absent from the array add nothing more, but the rule for reuse when values run out was not verified.
solution: Every appended element creates at least one new palindromic subarray, so k extra palindromes is a lower bound.
A new value x creates a palindrome of length >= 2 ending at the new position only if an earlier equal element sits at the matching distance with a palindromic interior.
Appending values that do not occur in the array (and are not yet appended) meets the lower bound exactly, as long as enough such values exist.
When too few unused values exist, choosing reused values needs an exact count of new palindromic suffixes; that rule was not derived here.
complexity: not derived
dry_run: Sample 2 (a = 2 2 2 2, k = 2): the unused values are 1 and 3; appending 1 then 3 adds only the single-character palindrome each, consistent with the sample answer 1 3.

brief: Save the Nature: sell n tickets in some order. The ticket sold at position i gives x% extra if i is a multiple of a, y% if a multiple of b, (x+y)% if both. Find the fewest tickets whose total contribution reaches k, or -1.
key_idea: Sell the most expensive tickets; for t sold tickets, give the largest percentages to the largest prices, and binary search the smallest t.
solution: Sort prices descending and build prefix sums.
For t sold tickets: both = t/lcm(a,b) slots get x+y, A-only = t/a - both get x, B-only = t/b - both get y, the rest get 0.
Pair the nonzero percentages in descending order with the top prices; the sum of price*percent is the contribution in price*percent units.
This total is non-decreasing in t, so binary search the smallest t with total >= 100*k; if t = n fails, print -1.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2 (top prices 200,200,200,100,...; x=10, a=2; y=15, b=3; k=107, so the target is 10700 units).

brief: Reverse the Rivers: n countries with k regions. After the flow, region j of country i holds the OR of the original values of region j over countries 1..i. For each query of conditions (region, < or >, c), find the smallest country satisfying all of them, or -1.
key_idea: The prefix OR of each region is non-decreasing in the country index, so each condition selects a prefix (for <) or a suffix (for >) of countries; intersect them with binary search.
solution: Precompute pref[i][j] = OR of a[1..i][j] for all countries i and regions j.
For a '<' condition on region r with value c, the valid countries form a prefix; binary search the last index with pref < c and set hi = min(hi, that index).
For a '>' condition, the valid countries form a suffix; binary search the first index with pref > c and set lo = max(lo, that index).
Answer lo if lo <= hi, else -1 (lo starts at 1 and hi at n).
complexity: O(nk) time and space for prefixes, O(log n) per condition
dry_run: Sample query 1: region 1 prefix ORs are 1, 5, 7. The condition '1 > 4' gives lo = 2; '1 < 6' gives hi = 2.
Region 2 prefix ORs are 3, 7, 7, so '2 < 8' keeps hi = 2. Answer 2, matching the sample.

brief: Friends stand at positions a_i in [0,x]. Choose k distinct integer teleport positions in [0,x] to maximize the minimum, over friends, of the distance to the nearest teleport.
key_idea: Binary search the answer D: the integers at distance >= D from every friend form O(n) disjoint intervals; D is feasible if they contain at least k integers.
solution: Sort and deduplicate the friend positions a_1 < ... < a_m.
For D >= 1 the allowed integers are [0, a_1 - D], the gaps [a_i + D, a_{i+1} - D], and [a_m + D, x]; these are disjoint.
The count is non-increasing in D; binary search the largest D >= 1 with count >= k. If none, D = 0 and the teleports are 0..k-1.
Print k integers from the allowed intervals.
complexity: O(n log n + n log x) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1 (friends 0,1,2,4; x=4; k=1): D=1 leaves the interval [3,3] (count 1); D=2 leaves nothing.
Output teleport 3, matching the sample answer 3.

brief: New Year Permutation: a permutation p and a symmetric 0/1 matrix A. You may swap p_i and p_j when A[i][j] = 1, any number of times. Output the lexicographically smallest reachable permutation.
key_idea: Positions linked by allowed swaps form components; inside a component the values can be arranged arbitrarily, so give the smallest values to the smallest positions.
solution: Union i and j whenever A[i][j] = 1 (disjoint-set union, n <= 300).
For each component, collect its positions in increasing order and its values.
Sort the values ascending and place the k-th smallest value at the k-th smallest position of that component.
Print the resulting permutation.
complexity: O(n^2 * alpha(n)) time to read the matrix and union, O(n) extra space
dry_run: Sample 2: the edges 1-3, 2-4, 2-5, 3-4, 4-5 connect all five positions into one component.
Values 4 2 1 5 3 sorted are 1 2 3 4 5, placed in position order: output 1 2 3 4 5, matching the sample.

brief: Sum in the tree: a rooted tree (root 1, parents p_i < i) with non-negative edge values a_v. s_v is the sum of a on the path from v to the root. Some s_v at even depth are erased; restore a minimizing the total sum of a, or print -1.
key_idea: Each erased even-depth s_v should be as large as possible: the minimum of its children's s (or its parent's s for a leaf); then check every a_v >= 0.
solution: Compute depths in one pass (root depth 1), since p_i < i.
For each erased even-depth vertex v: if it has children set s_v = min of their s (children are odd depth, so known); if it is a leaf set s_v = s_parent (a_v = 0).
Set a_1 = s_1 and a_v = s_v - s_parent(v) for v >= 2.
If any a_v < 0 print -1; otherwise print the sum of a_v.
complexity: O(n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 2 (parents 1 2 3 1; s = 1 -1 2 -1 -1): depths 1,2,3,4,2.
s_2 = min(s_3) = 2, s_4 = s_3 = 2, s_5 = s_1 = 1. Then a = 1, 1, 0, 0, 0 with sum 2, matching the sample.

brief: Remove the Substring (easy): t is a subsequence of s. Remove one contiguous substring of s so that t is still a subsequence of what remains; maximize the removed length.
key_idea: Removing s[l..r) keeps t a subsequence iff the greedy left match of t in s[0..l) plus the greedy right match of t in s[r..n) covers all of t.
solution: pre[l] = length of the longest prefix of t matched greedily inside s[0..l).
suf[r] = length of the longest suffix of t matched greedily from the right inside s[r..n).
The removal s[l..r) is valid iff pre[l] + suf[r] >= |t|.
Take the maximum of r - l over valid pairs (all pairs are checked since n <= 200).
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1 (s = bbaba, t = bb): pre[2] = 2 (keep 'bb'), suf[5] = 0, so 2 + 0 >= 2 is valid with r - l = 5 - 2 = 3.
Answer 3, matching the sample.

brief: Same Count One: n binary arrays of length m. An operation swaps the z-th element between two arrays. Make every array have the same number of ones with the fewest operations, or print -1.
key_idea: A swap preserves each column's total, so the total number of ones must be divisible by n; the minimum equals the total surplus, and every swap moves one unit from a surplus array to a deficit array.
solution: Let c_i be the ones in array i and S their sum. If S mod n != 0 print -1; else avg = S / n.
Pick an array hi with c > avg and lo with c < avg. A column z with a_hi[z] = 1 and a_lo[z] = 0 exists, since c_hi - c_lo such columns exist.
One pass over the columns swaps at such z until hi or lo reaches avg; repeat.
The count of swaps equals the total surplus, which is a lower bound because each swap lowers one surplus by 1.
complexity: O(n*m + n^2) time, O(n*m) space
dry_run: Sample 1: counts 3,1,2 with avg 2. hi = array 1 (surplus 1), lo = array 2 (deficit 1).
Column 1 has a_1 = 1 and a_2 = 0, so swap it: output 1 op '1 2 1', counts become 2,2,2, matching the sample count 1.

brief: Menorah: a row of n candles. Pressing a lit candle keeps it lit and toggles all others. Find the minimum number of presses that turns string a into string b, or -1.
key_idea: Not solved. With k presses and c_j presses on candle j, the final state satisfies b_j = a_j xor ((k - c_j) mod 2); the lit-before-press constraint and the minimum k were not resolved.
solution: Each press is a global toggle followed by re-toggling the pressed candle.
This gives the parity identity c_j = (k + a_j + b_j) mod 2 for every candle j.
Not derived: the minimum k that satisfies the parity identity together with the lit-before-press order constraint.
complexity: not derived
dry_run: Own example: a = 01, b = 11. Pressing candle 2 (lit) once toggles candle 1 from 0 to 1 and keeps candle 2 lit, giving 11 with 1 press, matching the sample answer 1.

brief: Stas and the Queue: n students with values a_i and b_i. The dissatisfaction of the student at position j is a(j-1) + b(n-j). Reorder the students to minimize the total.
key_idea: Each student's cost is j*(a-b) + (b*n - a); the constant part does not depend on order, and by the rearrangement inequality larger (a-b) goes to smaller positions.
solution: Rewrite the cost of student i at position j as j*(a_i - b_i) + (b_i*n - a_i).
Sum the constant parts over all students (order independent).
Sort students by a_i - b_i in descending order and assign positions 1..n in that order.
Print the constant plus the sum of j*(a-b) using 64-bit integers.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
dry_run: Constants: (2*3-4) + (3*3-2) + (1*3-6) = 6. Total 12, matching the sample.

brief: Compression and Expansion: a nested list of items whose numbers were overwritten so that each item keeps only its last number. Restore any valid nested list that could have produced the input and print each item in dotted form.
key_idea: Keep the current path as a stack of last numbers; a value 1 opens a deeper level, and any other value a pops back to the level whose last number is a-1 and replaces it with a.
solution: Keep the stack st of last numbers on the current path.
If a_i = 1, push 1 (a new nested level).
Otherwise pop until the top equals a_i - 1, then set the top to a_i.
After each item print the stack joined with dots.
complexity: O(n^2) time for printing (n <= 1000), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1 (1 1 2 3): stack [1] prints 1; push 1 prints 1.1; a=2 finds top 1 = a-1, replaced gives 1.2; a=3 replaces top 2 giving 1.3, matching the sample.

brief: Seating Arrangement (hard): x tables with s seats each. People arrive in a fixed order as I (must sit at an empty table), E (must sit at a non-empty table) or A (any table). Seat or turn away each person to maximize the number seated.
key_idea: A simple per-person greedy over (empty tables, free seats in occupied tables) is wrong: sample 6 needs the ambivert to open a table, so an exact choice procedure is required and was not derived.
solution: State: E = empty tables, F = free seats in occupied tables. An I needs E > 0; an E needs F > 0; an A needs F > 0 or E > 0.
Seating an I at an empty table gives F += s - 1 and E -= 1.
The rule 'an A takes an occupied seat first' gives only 2 on sample 6 (x=2, s=2, IAEE), where the answer is 4; so this rule is wrong.
An exact method (choice of when an A opens a table) was not derived here.
complexity: not derived
dry_run: Sample 6 (x=2, s=2, IAEE): the optimum seats I at table 1, A opens table 2, then E and E fill the two free seats, total 4.
The 'A takes occupied seat first' rule seats I and A only, total 2, which is why it fails.

brief: Li Hua and Chess (interactive): a king hides on an n x m board. You may ask at most 3 cells for the king's move distance (Chebyshev distance) and must then output the king's cell.
key_idea: Interactive problem; each Chebyshev answer confines the king to a square ring around the query, but a strategy that always uses at most 3 queries was not derived and cannot be tested offline.
solution: For a king at (x,y) and a query (r,c), the answer is max(|r-x|, |c-y|).
Each answer confines the king to a square ring centered on the query.
A 3-query strategy covering all boards was not derived; no code is recorded.
complexity: not derived
dry_run: Sample (3x4 board, king at (2,2)): query (2,3) gives max(0,1) = 1 and query (2,4) gives max(0,2) = 2, consistent with the sample responses; no algorithm traced.

brief: Walking Between Houses: start at house 1 and make exactly k moves, each to a different house, on a row of n houses. Decide whether the total walked distance can be exactly s and output one valid sequence.
key_idea: For n >= 3 the answer is YES iff k <= s <= k(n-1); build it with moves between houses 1 and n, one medium move for the remainder, then unit steps between two adjacent houses.
solution: If n = 2 the only moves are between 1 and 2, so the answer is YES iff s = k.
For n >= 3 print NO unless k <= s <= k(n-1). Let e = s - k, q = e / (n-2), rem = e mod (n-2).
Make q moves between house 1 and house n (each adds n-2 to the extra).
If rem > 0, add one move of length rem+1 from the current end: to rem+2 if at house 1, or to n-rem-1 if at house n.
Fill the remaining moves with unit steps alternating between the current house and a neighbour.
complexity: O(k) time and output, O(k) space
dry_run: Sample 1 (n=10, k=2, s=15): e = 13, q = 1, rem = 5. Move 1 -> 10 (distance 9); from 10 move to 4 (distance 6).
Total 15, output '10 4', matching the sample.

brief: Table Cut: an n x m table of 0/1 values. A cut from the top-left to the bottom-right corner moving only right or down splits the ones into a and T-a. Maximize a*(T-a) and output a cut path.
key_idea: Moving the cut by one cell changes a by 0 or 1, so every a from 0 to T is reachable; use a = floor(T/2) and build the path by flipping cells in a fixed order until the count matches.
solution: Let T be the total number of ones; the best product is floor(T/2) * ceil(T/2), so target a = floor(T/2).
Start from path D^n R^m (empty side). Flip cells in the order: column r = 0..m-1, row d = n-1 down to 0; each flip adds cell (d,r) and its value to a running count.
Stop at the first flip where the count equals a; the path is R^r D^d R D^(n-d) R^(m-r-1).
If a = 0 the path is D^n R^m. Print a*(T-a) and the path.
complexity: O(n*m) time, O(n*m) space
dry_run: Sample 3 (3x2 rows 10, 01, 11): T = 4, a = 2. Flips: (2,0) gives 1, (1,0) gives 1, (0,0) gives 2 and stop at r=0, d=0.
Path R D D D R, region count 2, product 2*2 = 4, matching the sample.

brief: Set To Max (easy): arrays a and b of length n. An operation picks a range, computes its maximum x and sets every element in the range to x. Decide whether a can be turned into b.
key_idea: Values only copy existing maxima, so b_i >= a_i is required; for b_i > a_i some j with a_j = b_i must reach i through a segment where all a <= b_i and all b >= b_i.
solution: If any a_i > b_i, answer NO.
For each i with a_i < b_i let v = b_i; look for j with a_j = v such that every k between i and j has a_k <= v and b_k >= v.
If no such j exists for some i, answer NO; otherwise YES.
Checking all pairs is O(n^2) per test, which fits since the sum of n^2 is at most 10^6.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(n) space per test
dry_run: Sample 5 (a = 1 1 2, b = 2 1 2): position 1 needs value 2; j = 3 has a_3 = 2, but inside the segment b_2 = 1 < 2, so NO, matching the sample.

brief: Weakened Common Divisor: n pairs (a_i, b_i). Find an integer greater than 1 that divides at least one number of every pair, or print -1.
key_idea: Any valid divisor must share a prime factor with a_1 or b_1, so test only those primes (at most about 20) against all pairs.
solution: Factor a_1 and b_1 by trial division up to sqrt (about 4.5*10^4).
Candidates are their distinct prime factors.
For each candidate p, check that p divides a_i or b_i for every pair.
Print the first valid candidate, else -1.
complexity: O(sqrt(max) + C*n) time with C <= about 20 candidates, O(1) extra space
dry_run: Sample 1 (17 18 / 15 24 / 12 15): candidates 17, 2, 3. 17 fails on pair 2; 2 divides 18, 24 and 12, so print 2.
2 is a valid answer (any valid divisor is accepted), though the sample shows 6.

brief: Fair: n towns in a connected graph, each producing one of k goods types. For each town find the minimum total road distance needed to bring at least s different types to it.
key_idea: Run one multi-source BFS per goods type; for each town, the answer is the sum of the s smallest distances over the types.
solution: For each type t (k <= 100) run BFS from all towns producing t to get dist_t[v].
For each town v collect dist_t[v] over all types t.
Sort these k values and sum the smallest s.
Print the sums for towns 1..n.
complexity: O(k*(n+m) + n*k*log k) time, O(n*k) space
dry_run: Sample 1, town 1: distances to types 1,2,3,4 are 0, 1, 1, 2 (type 3 at town 4, type 4 at town 3, type 2 at town 2).
Sum of the 3 smallest is 0 + 1 + 1 = 2, matching the first output value.

brief: Azamon Web Services: product name s and competitor name c (uppercase). Swap at most one pair of characters in s; print a resulting name strictly smaller than c, or ---.
key_idea: The smallest one-swap string: at the first position where a smaller letter appears later, swap with the last occurrence of the smallest such letter.
solution: Scan i from the left; let mn be the minimum of s[i+1..].
If mn < s[i], take the last index j > i with s[j] = mn, swap s[i] and s[j], and stop.
This gives the smallest reachable string (or s itself if no swap helps).
If it is smaller than c print it, else print ---.
complexity: O(L^2) time with the simple suffix scan (sum of L <= 5000), O(L) space
dry_run: Sample 1 (s = AZAMON, c = APPLE): position 1 'Z' has a later 'A' at index 2; swap gives AAZMON, which is smaller than APPLE; print AAZMON (any valid answer is accepted).
Sample 2 (c = AAAAAAAAAAALIBABA): AAZMON is larger, so print ---, matching the sample.

brief: Social Network: n people and d conditions (x_i, y_i) that must be connected by acquaintance chains. For each i, after William makes exactly i introductions while satisfying conditions 1..i, output the maximum number of acquaintances of one person.
key_idea: Use the largest condition-component as the hub: U unions are needed, the B = i - U spare introductions link further components (largest first) or add free people to the hub.
solution: After the first i conditions, union them in a DSU; U = number of successful unions (minimum introductions needed).
Spare introductions B = i - U.
Hub = largest component of size S_0, giving S_0 - 1; each of the next largest components adds its size if one spare introduction links it (up to B links).
Leftover spare introductions add one each to the hub while free people remain; cap the answer at n-1.
complexity: O(d * n log n) time (recomputed for each i), O(n) space
dry_run: Sample 1, i=6: one component of size 7, U = 6, B = 0; answer 7 - 1 = 6, matching.
Sample 2, i=6: components 4, 2, 2 with U = 5, B = 1; answer 3 + 2 = 5, matching the sample value 5.
